founder.name: Jeff Bezos
founder.title: Amazon founder
lines: Hi! Welcome to Day 1 — it's still Day 1 here.
Start with the customer and work backwards!
Most decisions are two-way doors — go try it.
Think long term. Really long term.
Want to read my letters? Every year has a lesson.
Stay curious and keep inventing.
Big wins pay for lots of experiments.
Frugal doesn't mean cheap — it means clever.

letters.author: Jeff Bezos
letters.title: It's All About the Long Term
lessons: Amazon decided to judge itself by long-term value, not next quarter's profit.
Obsess over customers: selection, ease of use and low prices win them.
It is "Day 1" — the internet (and Amazon) are just getting started.
Keep hiring a high bar of talented, owner-minded people.
letters.takeaway: Design for the long term: the cheapest-looking shortcut today often costs more over years — just like picking a managed service over a server you must babysit.
letters.quote: It's All About the Long Term.

letters.author: Jeff Bezos
letters.title: Raising the hiring bar
lessons: Customers are loyal only until someone offers a better service, so keep improving.
Setting a high bar for hiring is one of the most important choices a company makes.
Ask of every hire: will I admire them, will they raise the team average, could they be a superstar?
Stay focused on customers rather than competitors.
letters.takeaway: Great teams build great systems: the Bar Raiser idea still shapes how AWS hires.

letters.author: Jeff Bezos
letters.title: Building for the long haul
lessons: Amazon grew fast by investing ahead of demand in new stores and fulfilment.
The goal: be the most customer-centric company on Earth.
Big investments now can pay back for decades.
Stay close to what customers actually want.
letters.takeaway: Invest in foundations early — good architecture and automation compound over time.

letters.author: Jeff Bezos
letters.title: Surviving the dot-com crash
lessons: The stock price fell hard, but the business itself kept improving.
In the short run the market votes on popularity; in the long run it weighs real value.
Focus on things you control: customer experience, cost structure, cash.
Keep lowering prices and improving service in tough times.
letters.takeaway: When things break, measure what matters (latency, errors, cost) rather than reacting to noise.
letters.quote: Ouch. It's been a brutal year for many in the capital markets and certainly for Amazon.com shareholders.

letters.author: Jeff Bezos
letters.title: Lower prices, better experience
lessons: Amazon chose to pass cost savings to customers as lower prices.
Free cash flow — not just profit — shows how healthy the business is.
A better experience brings more customers, which lowers costs further: a flywheel.
Small improvements repeated every day add up.
letters.takeaway: Efficiency savings passed to customers is exactly how AWS has cut prices many times.

letters.author: Jeff Bezos
letters.title: What's good for customers is good for shareholders
lessons: Long-term shareholder value and customer value point the same way.
Free shipping offers and lower prices grew the business.
Opening the store to third-party sellers added selection.
Cost discipline makes low prices possible.
letters.takeaway: Serve customers first; the business results follow — a pattern AWS repeats with pay-as-you-go pricing.

letters.author: Jeff Bezos
letters.title: Long-term thinking
lessons: Make decisions by asking what they mean for the business years from now.
Some customer-friendly features (like reviews that can be negative) cost sales today but build trust.
Owners, not renters, take care of the long-term health of a company.
Patience is a competitive advantage.
letters.takeaway: Trust is earned over years: transparent pricing and honest docs keep AWS customers.

letters.author: Jeff Bezos
letters.title: Free cash flow per share
lessons: Amazon explained why free cash flow per share is its main financial measure.
Profit on paper can hide the cash a business really needs.
Capital-efficient growth lets you keep investing.
Explain your metrics clearly to the people who rely on them.
letters.takeaway: Pick the right metric: in the cloud, watch unit cost per request, not just the total bill.

letters.author: Jeff Bezos
letters.title: Data vs judgment
lessons: Many decisions can be made with data and experiments.
Some of the best decisions — like fast free shipping for members (Prime) — need judgment because the data can't prove them yet.
Be willing to make bold bets that look expensive at first.
Always tie the bet back to a better customer experience.
letters.takeaway: Use metrics where you can (CloudWatch!), but some architecture choices are judgment calls.

letters.author: Jeff Bezos
letters.title: Planting seeds for new businesses
lessons: New businesses take years to matter — plant seeds and be patient.
Amazon started Fulfillment by Amazon and Amazon Web Services (S3, EC2).
New ideas must have the chance to become big and to earn good returns.
Build on skills you already have, even when the idea looks unusual.
letters.takeaway: AWS itself was a seed: Amazon turned its own infrastructure skills into a service for everyone.

letters.author: Jeff Bezos
letters.title: Kindle and reinventing the book
lessons: Kindle was built to disappear in your hands so you get lost in reading.
Invent even when it disrupts your own business.
Start from what customers love and remove friction.
Take a long view on hardware and content together.
letters.takeaway: Don't protect old ways of doing things — AWS keeps launching services that replace older ones.

letters.author: Jeff Bezos
letters.title: Working backwards in a tough economy
lessons: During the financial crisis Amazon kept focusing on customers.
Start with customer needs and work backwards, rather than starting from your skills.
Long-term thinking lets you invest while others cut.
Stay frugal and keep improving costs.
letters.takeaway: Working backwards from the customer is how AWS writes a PR/FAQ before building a service.

letters.author: Jeff Bezos
letters.title: Goals that serve customers
lessons: Amazon sets hundreds of detailed goals each year, most about customer experience.
Few goals are about financial results; those follow from inputs.
Controllable inputs (speed, selection, price) drive outputs (revenue).
Review goals regularly and in detail.
letters.takeaway: Measure inputs you control: deployment frequency, error rates and latency lead to happy customers.

letters.author: Jeff Bezos
letters.title: Technology is the fundamental tool
lessons: Amazon described the computer science behind the store: distributed systems, machine learning, service-oriented architecture.
Invention is part of the culture and technology is its main tool.
AWS lets other developers use the same building blocks.
Customers benefit when engineers are free to experiment.
letters.takeaway: Service-oriented architecture — small independent services talking over APIs — is the idea behind microservices on AWS.

letters.author: Jeff Bezos
letters.title: The power of self-service platforms
lessons: Self-service platforms (Kindle Direct Publishing, FBA, AWS) let anyone build without asking permission.
Removing gatekeepers unleashes lots of experiments.
Invention works best when many people can try things cheaply.
Platforms create value for customers and for the people building on them.
letters.takeaway: An API is a self-service platform: no ticket needed to get a server or a bucket.

letters.author: Jeff Bezos
letters.title: Customer obsession, not competitor focus
lessons: Focus on customers rather than competitors — delight them before they ask.
Proactively lower prices and improve service even without pressure.
AWS kept cutting prices as it got more efficient.
Take ownership and think long term.
letters.takeaway: AWS price reductions are a direct example of passing efficiency to customers.

letters.author: Jeff Bezos
letters.title: Inventing on behalf of customers
lessons: A tour of many launches across Prime, devices and AWS in one year.
Keep inventing: most improvements come from many small launches.
Employees are encouraged to think like owners.
Listen to customers, but also invent for needs they can't express yet.
letters.takeaway: AWS ships hundreds of features a year — continuous delivery at company scale.

letters.author: Jeff Bezos
letters.title: Three big ideas: Marketplace, Prime and AWS
lessons: Amazon described three businesses customers love that can grow for a long time.
A great business is loved by customers, can grow big, earns good returns and lasts.
Third-party sellers, Prime membership and AWS reinforce each other.
Big ideas take years of patient work.
letters.takeaway: AWS became one of Amazon's "big ideas" — built from the company's own needs.

letters.author: Jeff Bezos
letters.title: Two-way doors: invention and failure
lessons: Most decisions are reversible "two-way doors" — make them fast.
A few are one-way doors that deserve slow, careful thought.
Failure and invention are inseparable twins; big wins pay for many experiments.
AWS grew faster than Amazon.com did at the same age.
letters.takeaway: Cloud makes most choices two-way doors: you can try an instance type and change it tomorrow.
letters.quote: But most decisions aren't like that – they are changeable, reversible – they're two-way doors.

letters.author: Jeff Bezos
letters.title: Day 1 vs Day 2
lessons: Day 2 is stasis followed by decline — so it is always Day 1.
Protect Day 1 with true customer obsession and resisting proxies (process is not the goal).
Embrace external trends quickly, such as machine learning.
Make high-velocity decisions; "disagree and commit" keeps things moving.
letters.takeaway: Beware process as a proxy: a green checklist is not the same as a secure, working system.

letters.author: Jeff Bezos
letters.title: High standards
lessons: Customers are never satisfied, so standards keep rising.
High standards are teachable and specific to each area.
Know what "great" looks like and how long it really takes (e.g. a great six-page memo).
High standards produce better products and a better culture.
letters.takeaway: Well-Architected reviews are a way to teach high standards for cloud systems.
letters.quote: One thing I love about customers is that they are divinely discontent.

letters.author: Jeff Bezos
letters.title: Intuition, curiosity and wandering
lessons: Third-party sellers grew to sell more than Amazon itself.
Big breakthroughs often come from wandering and following curiosity, not only efficiency.
Keep experiments big enough to matter as the company grows.
Invent for customers even when they don't ask.
letters.takeaway: Leave room to explore: many AWS services started from a curious team trying something new.

letters.author: Jeff Bezos
letters.title: Meeting a pandemic
lessons: Written as COVID-19 spread: employee safety and serving customers came first.
Amazon described the Climate Pledge to reach net-zero carbon by 2040.
Upskilling programmes to help employees learn new skills.
Long-term thinking helps in a crisis.
letters.takeaway: Elastic cloud capacity let many businesses survive the sudden changes of 2020.

letters.author: Jeff Bezos
letters.title: Create more than you consume
lessons: A company must create more value than it consumes — for shareholders, employees, customers and sellers.
Amazon added two Leadership Principles: Earth's Best Employer and Success and Scale Bring Broad Responsibility.
Differentiation is survival: resist the pull to become typical.
Bezos's last letter as CEO before handing over to Andy Jassy.
letters.takeaway: Great platforms create more value for their builders than they charge — measure your value, not just your cost.
letters.quote: If you want to be successful in business (in life, actually), you have to create more than you consume.

letters.author: Andy Jassy
letters.title: Still Day 1: iterative innovation
lessons: Jassy's first letter: the fulfilment network doubled in about two years to meet pandemic demand.
Invention is iterative — keep improving products over many years.
Launch "minimum lovable products" quickly, then keep listening.
Small, autonomous single-threaded teams move fastest.
letters.takeaway: AWS services start small and improve release after release — ship early, iterate often.

letters.author: Andy Jassy
letters.title: Lean times, long-term bets
lessons: Amazon cut costs and regionalised its fulfilment network to deliver faster and cheaper.
Hard decisions now protect the long-term investments.
Big bets continued: AWS, healthcare, Project Kuiper and large language models.
Custom chips (Graviton, Trainium, Inferentia) lower costs for customers.
letters.takeaway: Cost optimisation and innovation go together — right-size, then reinvest the savings.

letters.author: Andy Jassy
letters.title: Building in primitives
lessons: Build simple, foundational building blocks ("primitives") that builders can combine.
AWS services are primitives — flexible pieces rather than one rigid product.
Generative AI has three layers: chips/compute, services like Bedrock, and applications.
Faster delivery through a regionalised network.
letters.takeaway: Think in primitives: combine S3, Lambda and DynamoDB instead of waiting for one perfect product.

letters.author: Andy Jassy
letters.title: The world's largest startup
lessons: Keep asking "why?" to challenge assumptions and improve.
Operate like a startup: speed, scrappiness, ownership and few layers.
Generative AI will reinvent nearly every customer experience.
Keep investing in delivery speed, healthcare, Kuiper and Alexa+.
letters.takeaway: Small teams with real ownership ship faster — the two-pizza team idea at scale.

letters.author: Andy Jassy
letters.title: Speed, inflections and parallel paths
lessons: We are living through some of the biggest technology inflections of our lifetimes.
Speed matters disproportionately, and the whole culture must embrace it.
When the best route is unclear, pursue parallel paths and learn from each.
Jassy shares lessons from his decades at Amazon for handling big changes.
letters.takeaway: Experiment in parallel: the cloud makes it cheap to try two designs and keep the winner.

items.name: Customer Obsession
items.explain: Start with the customer and work backwards; earn and keep their trust.
items.awsExample: Most of the AWS roadmap comes from what customers ask for.

items.name: Ownership
items.explain: Think long term and act for the whole company, never "that's not my job".
items.awsExample: Under the shared responsibility model you own your data and IAM settings.

items.name: Invent and Simplify
items.explain: Look for new ideas everywhere and make things simpler.
items.awsExample: Lambda removed servers from the job of running code.

items.name: Are Right, A Lot
items.explain: Good judgement and instincts, while seeking views that challenge your beliefs.
items.awsExample: Architecture reviews invite dissent before a design ships.

items.name: Learn and Be Curious
items.explain: Never stop learning and exploring new possibilities.
items.awsExample: AWS Skill Builder and certifications — like this city!

items.name: Hire and Develop the Best
items.explain: Raise the bar with every hire and help people grow.
items.awsExample: Bar Raisers take part in Amazon interview loops.

items.name: Insist on the Highest Standards
items.explain: Keep raising the bar and fix defects so they stay fixed.
items.awsExample: The Well-Architected Framework sets a high bar for cloud designs.

items.name: Think Big
items.explain: Create a bold direction that inspires results.
items.awsExample: Amazon Leo (formerly Project Kuiper) and custom chips like Graviton.

items.name: Bias for Action
items.explain: Speed matters; many decisions are reversible, so don't over-study.
items.awsExample: Try a new instance type today — you can switch back tomorrow.

items.name: Frugality
items.explain: Do more with less; constraints breed invention.
items.awsExample: Savings Plans, Spot Instances and AWS price cuts.

items.name: Earn Trust
items.explain: Listen, speak candidly and treat others respectfully.
items.awsExample: Public post-event summaries after major AWS outages.

items.name: Dive Deep
items.explain: Stay close to details and check when metrics and stories disagree.
items.awsExample: CloudWatch and X-Ray help you trace a problem to its root.

items.name: Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit
items.explain: Challenge decisions you disagree with, then commit fully once decided.
items.awsExample: Debate in the design review; then everyone builds the chosen design.

items.name: Deliver Results
items.explain: Focus on the key inputs and deliver with the right quality, on time.
items.awsExample: Services launch with an SLA customers can rely on.

items.name: Strive to be Earth’s Best Employer
items.explain: Create a safer, more productive, more inclusive and fun workplace.
items.awsExample: Upskilling programmes for Amazonians to move into tech roles.

items.name: Success and Scale Bring Broad Responsibility
items.explain: Be humble about impact and leave things better than you found them.
items.awsExample: The Climate Pledge and the sustainability pillar of Well-Architected.

mechanisms.name: Working Backwards (PR/FAQ)
mechanisms.explain: Before building, write the launch press release and FAQ from the customer's point of view.
steps: Name the customer and the problem in one sentence.
Write a one-page press release as if the product launched today.
Add a customer quote and how to get started.
Answer the hard questions in an FAQ (cost, risks, "so what?").
Review, rewrite, repeat — only build once the story is clear.
mechanisms.awsExample: Many AWS services began as a PR/FAQ before any code was written.

mechanisms.name: Two-pizza teams
mechanisms.explain: Small, autonomous teams — small enough to be fed by two pizzas — that own a service end to end.
steps: Keep the team small (fewer than ~10 people).
Give it one clear owner and mission.
Let it own its service, from code to on-call.
Talk to other teams through APIs, not meetings.
mechanisms.awsExample: Each AWS service is built and run by small teams that own it.

mechanisms.name: Day 1 vs Day 2
mechanisms.explain: Stay a "Day 1" company: customer obsessed, fast and inventive; Day 2 is slow decline.
steps: Obsess over customers, not process.
Resist proxies — a metric is not the goal.
Embrace outside trends quickly.
Decide fast: most doors are two-way.
mechanisms.awsExample: Adopting generative AI quickly across AWS is a Day 1 move.

mechanisms.name: The six-page narrative
mechanisms.explain: Meetings start with everyone silently reading a written narrative instead of slides.
steps: Write up to six pages of full sentences.
State the goal, the approach and the decision needed.
Start the meeting with ~15–20 minutes of silent reading.
Discuss questions, then decide.
mechanisms.awsExample: Designs and yearly plans at AWS are written as narratives.

mechanisms.name: Correction of Error (COE)
mechanisms.explain: A blameless write-up after something goes wrong, so the fix is a mechanism, not a person.
steps: Describe what happened, with a timeline.
Measure the customer impact.
Ask "why?" five times to reach the root cause.
List action items with owners and dates.
Share what was learned.
mechanisms.awsExample: AWS teams write COEs after operational events and share the lessons.

launches.note: Storage for the internet — AWS's first big service.
Rent virtual servers by the hour.
A fully managed NoSQL database for any scale.
A data warehouse announced at the first re:Invent.
Run code on events without servers — the start of serverless.
Run Docker containers on a managed cluster.
Query files in S3 with plain SQL.
Image analysis with deep learning as an API.
Build, train and deploy ML models.
A serverless event bus for apps and SaaS.
A generative AI assistant for work and for AWS.
Deploy and operate AI agents securely at scale.
